newsitem.title: USA: Cabinet, budget, strategy head Clinton agenda.
newsitem.headline: Cabinet, budget, strategy head Clinton agenda.

text.p: President Bill Clinton returns on Sunday to the White House to face an array of tasks: selecting his Cabinet, drafting the budget and deciding the opening strategy for his second term.

Having spent most of the past two weeks out of Washington -- including a 12-day trip to the Asia-Pacific region and a long Thanksgiving weekend at the Camp David presidential retreat -- Clinton gets down to serious business this week.

Heading his agenda is finding replacements for seven Cabinet officers, including the secretaries of state and defence, who announced after Clinton's victory over Republican Bob Dole in the Nov. 5 election that they would leave office.
One administration official said Clinton's first move is likely to be the reorganization of his national security team.

While hinting announcements could come as early as this week, officials were reluctant to be precise, noting Clinton hoped originally to make these decisions before leaving for Asia on November 15 but had already postponed them once.
"His thinking (is) much more advanced in the national security area," said one administration official, suggesting Clinton may unveil these choices first and as a group.
"It is more likely to be a multiple announcement -- not clear who and how many," he added.

The president must decide who will take the spots vacated by Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Defence Secretary William Perry, while weighing whether to keep on National Security Adviser Tony Lake.

Clinton returned from Asia on Wednesday, meeting for three hours with incoming chief of staff Erskine Bowles to talk over the Cabinet before leaving for a long Thanksgiving holiday weekend at Camp David.
He was scheduled to return to the White House later on Sunday.
Beyond personnel, Clinton has a range of substantive matters to take up, among them sending a budget to Congress, where Republicans control both houses.

He has also singled out two areas where he wants to pass legislation that is bound to be controversial: amending the welfare law passed earlier this year and changing the system by which political campaigns are financed.
Balancing the budget has been Washington's chief political battleground for the past two years, prompting two government shutdowns when Clinton and Congress could not come to terms.

Having won re-election in part by tarring Republicans for the unpopular shutdowns and by portraying them as seeking to cut the popular Medicare health care programme for the elderly, Clinton now faces a decidedly wary Congress.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said one administration action might be to admit that the rate of growth in Medicare spending must be slowed, describing this as the White House "taking more of the hit" for reining in the programme.
"(The) Republicans are being very cautious. You frankly wouldn't expect them to move yet because they're just getting organised," he added.

Franklin Raines, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, admitted the challenge of dealing with the new Congress when describing his preliminary talks on balancing the budget with Republicans over the past few weeks.
"Everyone informs me that the path will be longer rather than shorter," Raines said. "I have merely suggested that the earlier we start, no matter how long it is, we'll get it done sooner."
